newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Congo's Kabila to unveil new government - aide.
newsitem.headline: Congo's Kabila to unveil new government - aide.

text.p: Self-proclaimed president Laurent Kabila prepared to unveil his administration for the new Democratic Republic of Congo on Thursday, aides said.
As part of moves to choose his new team, Kabila also set a much-awaited meeting with radical opposition chief Etienne Tshisekedi, who has an army of fanatical supporters in the slums of Kinshasa.

"They're going to meet ... We're waiting for the security services to come here to take Mr Tshisekedi to Kabila's residence for the face-to-face," Kabila's cabinet chief Dieudonne Nyengela told Reuters at the politician's home.

Kabila's top aide met Tshisekedi on Wednesday for talks on forging a broad-based administration -- as demanded by foreign governments -- to replace the regime of Zaire's dictator Mobutu Sese Seko, toppled by Kabila's AFDL guerrillas at the weekend.
Kabila arrived in Kinshasa on Tuesday, the day he had promised to announce his administration. A senior aide said an announcement could come later on Thursday.
"We are finalising things. By the end of the day we may have an announcement," the secretary-general of Kabila's office, Moise Myarugabo, told Reuters.

Despite Wednesday's meeting between Tshisekedi and Kabila's number two, Deogratias Bugera, there was no indication that Tshisekedi, sacked twice as prime minister by Mobutu, would be included in the incoming government.
However, his fanatical followers from the capital's teeming shantytowns expect him to be Kabila's prime minister.
About 300 of them gathered outside Tshisekedi's Limete district home on Thursday, as they have daily this week, hailing their leader.
The United States, which joined South Africa in mediating in the Zaire conflict, has been working behind the scenes to bring the country's two strongmen together.
"We have a facilitating role. We are able to get in touch with both sides," U.S. embassy spokesman Joao Escodi told Reuters. "Now they have to do the talking. We're not involved in the talks."
As Kabila prepared for the tough task of running the chaotic country the size of Western Europe, South Africa said it was willing to offer technical advice and expertise to the new government.

Ricky Naidoo, a spokesman for Deputy President Thabo Mbeki, said South Africa would coordinate assistance from African and other states to ensure that Kabila had immediate access to the advice and expertise he would need to start rebuilding the Democratic Republic of Congo, formerly Zaire.

"Now that the first stage of the peace process is over, we cannot simply pack our bags and walk away. South Africa still has a critical role to play in terms of sharing our expertise," he told Reuters.
Naidoo said Kabila had asked South Africa to contact the World Bank on the technical assistance that might be available to help the country to rebuild its fiscal infrastructure.

At the same time, he said, joint United Nations and Organisation of African Unity envoy Mohamed Sahnoun would contact Western governments and funding agencies on direct financial help that might be available.
President Jacques Chirac told South African head of state Nelson Mandela on Thursday that France hoped the former Zaire would move towards democracy under Kabila.

Former colonial ruler Belgium said it would send its special envoy for Africa's Great Lakes region to meet the new leaders in Kinshasa but will not resume cooperation unless certain conditions -- notably progress towards democarcy -- are met.
